title: CAG
lead: Often called the ==‘Fourth Pillar’== of accountability alongside Legislature, Executive and Judiciary — and the ==‘friend, philosopher and guide’== to the Public Accounts Committee.

items: ==Art 148==: CAG appointed by the President, removable ==only like a Supreme Court judge== (impeachment for proved misbehaviour or incapacity) — ensuring independence from executive control.
==Art 149==: Parliament prescribes duties and powers — currently the ==CAG's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971==.
==Art 150==: President prescribes ==accounting formats== for Union and States ==on CAG's advice==.
==Art 151==: reports on Union accounts to the ==President== (laid before Parliament); on State accounts to the ==Governor== (laid before the State Legislature).
==Art 279==: CAG ==certifies net proceeds of taxes== for Centre–State distribution.
==Salary charged on the Consolidated Fund of India== — not subject to annual vote, safeguarding financial independence.

head: Type
Description
rows: ==Financial (regularity) audit==
Verifies accuracy and fairness of financial statements; whether transactions conform to law, rules and authority.
Compliance audit
Adherence to laws, rules, regulations and government orders.
==Performance audit (VFM)==
Assesses ==economy, efficiency and effectiveness== — whether outcomes justify expenditure.
Audit of autonomous bodies/PSUs
Government companies (==s.143, Companies Act 2013==) and statutory corporations.
==Environmental/social audit==
Emerging area — environmental compliance and social-sector delivery (MGNREGA, Swachh Bharat).
IT/systems audit
Computerised government systems, e-governance platforms, cybersecurity of financial systems.

items: ==Post-facto nature== — audits occur after expenditure, limiting real-time correction.
==Delayed tabling of reports== — months or years later, diluting relevance and public salience.
==Limited follow-up== — ==no binding power to enforce recommendations==; depends on PAC and executive responsiveness.
==Coverage gaps== — ==PPPs, autonomous societies and NGOs== receiving government funds often fall outside effective reach.
==Capacity constraints== — shortage of trained personnel for defence procurement, IT systems, complex financial instruments.
==Political weaponisation== — findings (2G, Coalgate) reduced to political slugfests rather than systemic correction.
==Appointment opacity== — appointed solely by the executive, ==without a broad-based collegium==.
==State-level neglect== — state reports receive far less scrutiny due to ==weaker state PACs==.
==No pre-audit for major contracts== — India lacks strong ==ex-ante financial control== compared to some OECD SAIs.

head: Audit
Outcome
rows: ==2G Spectrum Scam (2010)==

Flagged arbitrary ==first-come-first-served== allocation without auction, estimating massive presumptive loss — led to ==SC cancellation of licences== and a shift to auction-based resource allocation.
==Coal Block Allocation ‘Coalgate’ (2012)==
Highlighted opaque allocation without competitive bidding — SC ==cancelled over 200 allocations (2014)==.
Commonwealth Games 2010
Uncovered ==cost overruns, procurement irregularities, inflated contracts== — fed into PAC investigations and prosecutions.
==Rafale Deal Audit (2019)==
Examined defence pricing benchmarks — illustrating the CAG's ==expanding but contested== role in sensitive defence contracts.
Ayushman Bharat / state scheme audits
Flagged ==beneficiary duplication, fund diversion== and implementation gaps.

head: Case
Holding
rows: [[Association of Unified Telecom Service Providers v. UoI (2014)]]
Upheld the CAG's authority to ==audit private telecom providers== to the extent of their ==revenue-sharing arrangements== with the government.
[[Centre for PIL v. UoI (2012)]] — 2G Spectrum
Relied heavily on CAG findings of arbitrary allocation and ==cancelled 122 telecom licences==.
[[Manohar Lal Sharma v. UoI (2014)]] — Coal Blocks
Building on CAG findings, declared ==214 coal block allocations illegal and arbitrary==.
[[S. Subramaniam Balaji v. Govt of TN (2013)]]
Referenced CAG-style financial scrutiny standards in discussing ==transparent state expenditure accounting==.

head: Country
Practice
rows: ==UK — National Audit Office==
Value-for-money audits with ==mandatory government response within a fixed timeframe==; strong PAC linkage.
==USA — GAO==
Reports ==directly to Congress==; publishes a ==‘High-Risk List’== tracking vulnerable programmes with continuous follow-up until resolved.
==Germany — Bundesrechnungshof==
==Real-time and concurrent audit inputs into budget-making==, not just post-facto.
Canada — Auditor General
Strong ==‘sunset review’== mechanism requiring audited departments to report corrective action within set deadlines.

items: ==Institutionalise real-time/concurrent audit== for large infrastructure and defence contracts
==Mandatory Action Taken Reports== with legally binding timelines — the ==GAO High-Risk List== follow-up model
==Broaden the appointment process== — a collegium including the CJI and Leader of Opposition
==Expand audit jurisdiction== to PPPs, large NGOs and autonomous bodies receiving substantial public funds
==Strengthen technical capacity== — forensic accountants, IT auditors, defence procurement experts, not only generalist IAAS cadre
==Depoliticise report handling== — structured, non-adversarial PAC hearings
==Strengthen state-level PACs== through capacity-building and staffing
==Leverage AI-driven anomaly detection== on large-scale financial data, as GAO and NAO increasingly do

blocks.text: The CAG is not merely the government's accountant, but democracy's financial conscience — ensuring that every rupee raised in the people's name is spent with legality, prudence and public purpose.
